sections.title: Bank Credit Metrics
sections.subtitle: Asset quality and capital adequacy -- annual rows only; the regulator does not require interim disclosure of every ratio

charts.title: Capital Adequacy Ratios
charts.annotation: Regulatory minimums for a domestic systemically important bank are roughly 8.5% CET1 and 11.5% total capital; PSBC's FY2025 CET1 of ~10.5% reflects the RMB130bn A-share placement anchored by the Ministry of Finance.

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Operating income here is net interest income plus fee and other income less operating expenses and credit impairment; net income is after tax.

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): the gap between operating and net income is driven mainly by the deposit agency fee paid to China Post Group (~RMB110-112bn/yr, roughly 30% of operating income) -- the single largest opex line and a cost structure no other large Chinese bank bears, since PSBC rents rather than owns most of its ~40,000-outlet network.

What to watch:

  • Whether agency-fee renegotiations (adjusted again in Q1 2026) are showing up as slower opex growth
  • Credit impairment charges rising faster than operating income, which would signal the bank is reserving against the asset-quality drift shown below

nim.title: Net interest margin
nim.content:
Net interest margin (NIM) is net interest income divided by average interest-earning assets -- the spread a bank earns between what it pays for deposits/funding and what it earns on loans and securities.

For PSBC: NIM is the bank's dominant revenue driver and has nearly halved since 2021 (2.36% to 1.63% by H1-2026) as LPR cuts and mortgage repricing outpaced deposit-cost reductions. PSBC's retail/rural deposit-heavy, lower-yielding loan mix historically gives it a thinner NIM than joint-stock banks, so it has less room to absorb further compression.

What to watch:

  • Whether NIM stabilizes or keeps falling as PBOC policy stays accommodative
  • Deposit repricing lag versus asset repricing after each LPR cut

assetQuality.title: Asset quality: NPL ratio and allowance coverage
assetQuality.content:
NPL ratio is non-performing loans as a percentage of total loans; allowance coverage is loan-loss allowances as a percentage of NPLs -- the cushion available if those loans default.

For PSBC: both lines have moved the wrong way since 2021 -- NPL ratio up from 0.82% to 1.00% (H1-2026), allowance coverage down from 419% to roughly 215-228% -- narrowing the buffer against a Chinese property/SME credit downturn even though absolute asset quality remains strong by global bank standards.

What to watch:

  • NPL ratio continuing to climb each year rather than stabilizing
  • Allowance coverage falling toward 150% (the regulatory floor for most Chinese banks) rather than holding its current multiple-hundred-percent buffer

capitalRatios.title: Capital adequacy ratios
capitalRatios.content:
CET1 ratio and total capital ratio measure a bank's core and total loss-absorbing capital against risk-weighted assets.

For PSBC: as one of China's four largest state banks, PSBC is subject to higher regulatory minimums (roughly 8.5% CET1, 11.5% total capital for a D-SIB) than smaller lenders. The FY2025 RMB130bn A-share private placement, anchored by the Ministry of Finance as part of Beijing's RMB500bn recapitalization of the big-four state banks, lifted CET1 by ~0.96pp to ~10.5% -- a government-backed capital cushion, not organic retention.

What to watch:

  • Whether capital ratios drift back down as risk-weighted assets grow faster than retained earnings
  • Dividend payout relative to capital generation -- a bank paying out more than it earns in capital is drawing down its buffer

costToIncome.title: Cost-to-income ratio
costToIncome.content:
Cost-to-income ratio is operating expenses divided by operating income -- the standard bank efficiency metric.

For PSBC: this ratio is structurally elevated by the deposit agency fee paid to China Post Group for use of its ~40,000-outlet network, a cost competitors who own their branches outright do not bear. The ratio has improved from 64% toward 62% (FY2025) and 50.6% (H1-2026, on a different presentation basis) as management's 'Seven Major Reforms' and outlet-efficiency push, plus proactive downward adjustments to the agency fee rate, take effect.

What to watch:

  • Whether improvement continues or stalls once easy agency-fee renegotiation gains are exhausted
  • Digital/AI initiatives (the 'Youzhi' financial LLM) actually lowering headcount-driven costs, not just the agency fee line

returns.title: Return on equity and return on average assets
returns.content:
ROE is net income over average shareholders' equity; ROAA is net income over average total assets -- the two standard bank profitability yardsticks.

For PSBC: both are compressed by the same NIM pressure that squeezes operating income, and ROE in particular was diluted by the FY2025 A-share placement (more equity, same near-term earnings). A state-directed recapitalization that lowers ROE while raising the capital cushion is a deliberate regulatory trade-off, not a sign of a worsening franchise.

What to watch:

  • ROE trend once the placement's dilution anniversarizes
  • ROAA versus peer state banks -- PSBC's retail deposit funding advantage should show up here if NIM stabilizes

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Postal Savings Bank of China Co., Ltd. (PSBC): the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
